item.title: ‘I’m still trying to find out who I am’: the little-understood plight of Forgotten Australians
item.description: They number more than half a million, yet the ongoing trauma from their time in orphanages and institutions remains poorly known When Judy Leonard entered the orphanage, she was given a bed with a number. That was how the staff would refer to her. Not by her name, or even by one of the cruel nicknames the other children gave her, but by her allocated space in the dormitory: C2. “I would like the readers to close their eyes,” Judy says now, “and imagine that it was them at age nine.” Continue reading...

item.title: De la Fuente adamant there is no racism in Spain despite England reminder to players
item.description: England’s first game in Madrid since racist abuse in 2004 De la Fuente tells Tuchel ‘we’re not racists, none of us’ Luis de la Fuente has told Thomas Tuchel there is no racism in Spain after the England coach’s admission that he would remind his players of the anti-racism protocol prior to their meeting at the Metropolitano on Sunday night. This will be the first time the countries play each other in Madrid since some of England’s black players were subjected to racist abuse in a match at the Santiago Bernabéu in 2004 . And although England have returned to Spain three times without incident since then, twice in Seville and once in Alicante, Tuchel was asked about going back in the buildup to Sunday’s game. The England coach replied that England “will not expect anything [untoward]” but also said: “maybe we take our five minutes to inform the players about the protocol if there is a precedent [in Madrid].” Continue reading...

item.title: Five-try Will Joseph equals record as England steamroller Japan
item.description: England 78-15 Japan Steve Borthwick’s men score 13 tries Not every game of rugby can deliver a result for the ages. Admittedly, England do not score 13 tries every week but even if the hosts had run up 150 points they would have struggled to eclipse this weekend’s remarkable events in Cardiff and Paris. That said, in the annals of one-sided contests on this famous old stretch of turf, there have been few to match this virtual procession. To say Japan came a distant second is to be polite in the extreme. From the moment Will Joseph collected a hat-trick of tries inside the game’s opening 20 minutes it was simply a question of how many points England would rack up and, to their credit, Maro Itoje’s side tucked into the free buffet with relish. Joseph, playing only his second Test, claimed a record-equalling five tries as his side comfortably topped their previous highest score against the Brave Blossoms. Continue reading...

item.title: Wales bury 73-year All Blacks hoodoo with seismic victory over New Zealand
item.description: Wales 35-28 New Zealand Home side secure first win over All Blacks since 1953 Just when you expect it the least. By what wild logic did Wales choose now to pull off a victory 73 years in the seeking? There may have been only 55,000 in Cardiff’s great stadium for this first win over New Zealand since 1953, but judging by the noise alone, Wales are back. They had managed five wins in 31 Tests since the last World Cup, all of them against teams outside the top eight, and they choose now to beat the All Blacks. An extraordinary defensive display for the last half-hour kept wave after wave of New Zealand attacks at bay, each feat of heroism greeted as if the most sublime of tries by JPR, Gareth, Shane or JJ. None of those ever tasted this, but now a new generation of Welshmen, still young and hopeful, can add a win over the All Blacks to their CV. Continue reading...

item.title: I felt nothing but numbness at my dad’s death – but then I read the book he gave me on my wedding day

I laughed as I cried, and realised there’s no right way to go through the grieving process I expected to break. But I felt nothing. I did not cry, nor struggle to sleep. I seldom thought of him. I felt only guilt about how little I felt. Ours was a complex relationship. As a teen, I often resented my dad, occasionally despised him. I expected the world and found disappointment. But, as I grew older, I understood that he had struggles of his own. I learned to appreciate his decency and humour, his ability to make everyone laugh with only a few words. I loved my dad, from the first time he held me to the last time I held him. But still, as weeks turned into months, I struggled to grieve. But during the Vietnam war, a specialized patrol of army volunteers became critical to the US military effort. Known as long-range reconnaissance patrols, or LRRPs, these small teams of six to eight soldiers were dropped behind enemy lines to track supply routes and hostile positions, sometimes for days at a time. Stealth was essential. Their job was to identify targets and call in the cavalry, usually in the form of airstrikes, while avoiding direct engagement with enemy forces to preserve their cover. item.title: Barbara Kingsolver: ‘What does love feel like? At 16, breaking the speed limit. Years later, a warm bath’
item.description: The author on the FBI tapping her phone, teaching herself to read aged three, and why she knits in meetings Born in Maryland, in the US, Barbara Kingsolver, 71, won a music scholarship to DePauw University in Indiana. She became a journalist and published her first novel, The Bean Trees, in 1988. Her award-winning books include The Poisonwood Bible, The Lacuna and Demon Copperhead, which was published in 2022 and won the Pulitzer, the James Tait Black prize and the Women’s prize for fiction. In 2025, she founded the Higher Ground Women’s Recovery Residence in Lee County, Virginia, where the novel is set. Her latest novel is Partita . She lives in Virginia with her second husband and has two children. When were you happiest? Right after the births of my children. item.title: King Æthelstan founded England in the year 927. Why don’t we celebrate that anniversary? | Tom Holland
item.description: Nearly 1,100 years ago, the nation’s first king drove out the ‘heathen’ Vikings, declared war on starvation and made ‘Englalonde’ what it is today On 4 July, the United States celebrated its 250th birthday with all the razzmatazz and dazzle characteristic of an American public occasion. Next summer, on 12 July, England will be celebrating the 1,100th anniversary of the event that, more than any other, marked the founding of the country – but of razzmatazz and dazzle there will be, I suspect, very little. The great turning point took place on 12 July 927, beside the river Eamont in what today is Cumbria. Here, amid an untamed wilderness of mountains and lakes, the most powerful king in Britain had summoned other kings and lords from across the island to meet him for a summit. Continue reading...

item.title: Power creates wars; wars create power. But these compelling acts of storytelling are breaking the loop | Charlotte Higgins
item.description: Artists’ acts of remembrance about destruction and violence defy the dominant narratives of heroism and sacrifice The way stories are told about wars really matters. It is a point powerfully made by the classical scholar Alice König who, in her work on ancient and modern warfare, points out that the way war is depicted and narrativised feeds into the way wars are actually conducted. Creating and absorbing a story (whether that is told in prose or poetry, or offered by an artwork or memorial) is more than packaging or reflecting on the past; it is about generating images and expectations, and about envisioning the future. Stories, she argues, influence real-world behaviours. The war correspondent Christina Lamb has also made this connection in relation to sexual violence in conflict: depictions of war from Homer onwards show that women have always been trafficked and raped, used as bargaining chips and spolia, their bodies made battlefields. A rough halt hewn out of the mountainside, with no ticket office, no waiting room, no sign of human habitation – just a single platform in the wilderness. On the far side of the track, a shimmering turquoise lake flanked by pine forests. Ahead – the only way out – a rocky trail snaking up the limestone cliff. My husband and I had first strayed into this western corner of Catalonia – Pallars Jussà – on our honeymoon road trip 21 years earlier. Seduced by its dramatic landscape of canyons, lakes, crumbling ruins and the formidable Noguera Pallaresa river thundering south from the Pyrenees, we had vowed to return one day. item.title: The Guardian view on press freedom: authoritarians target journalism because it matters | Editorial
item.description: From Cairo to Moscow to Washington, governments are turning up the pressure on media workers Lina Attalah is an influential Egyptian journalist. Yet until last month, even she was unaware of a major and concerning piece of news: her own conviction. In 2024, a court issued her a one-year sentence for “spreading false news” and running a website without a licence – which she had repeatedly sought to obtain – after trying her in absentia, even though she was in the country. Ms Attalah learned of the case only after she was separately tried in October , resulting in a large fine and an order for the closure of the Mada Masr website. She faces retrial later this month. Meanwhile, the entire newsroom of the fact-checking website Matsadash remain in detention weeks after authorities snatched the six journalists on charges including joining and financing a terrorist group and spreading false news. item.title: The Guardian view on M John Harrison’s Booker win: a new frontier for science fiction | Editorial
item.description: The End of Everything is a novel for our age of permacrisis. Genre boundaries belong to the past “Science fiction will never be Literature with a capital ‘L,’” began a New York Times review of Margaret Atwood’s novel Oryx and Crake back in 2003. Now, the seemingly impossible has happened – M John Harrison’s The End of Everything is the first science fiction novel to win the Booker prize. Fans have hailed this as a victory for a long-marginalised genre. The author himself was not so sure. “Writing science fiction is the last thing I want to do,” he said with characteristic iconoclasm at an event before the prize. The sci-fi v literary or “mainstream” fiction debate is as endless and battle-strewn as a fantasy saga. The late Ursula K Le Guin, a giant of the form, famously took Atwood to task for her reluctance to use the term science fiction for some of her novels, including Oryx and Crake: “She doesn’t want the literary bigots to shove her into the literary ghetto.” Harrison doesn’t wan

item.title: Storm Charles causes floods and flight cancellations across southern Europe
item.description: Heavy rain and strong winds have also caused disruption across British Columbia, Canada, over the last week Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninsula this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm (13.97in) in 12 hours. In Lisbon, 183 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, about a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations. After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. item.description: (Erased Tapes) Dreamy, reverb-laden arrangements, virtuosic vocals and echoes of PJ Harvey and Massive Attack make this disarming debut a one-of-a-kind creation Since the release of her debut EP, Qasr , in 2024, south Asian-American vocalist and composer Sheherazaad has developed a distinctive take on the classical singing of her heritage. item.title: Snoh Aalegra: Legendary Love review – raw R&B talent restrained by reverence for the greats
item.description: (Stem) Her truly remarkable, Sade-ish voice is hypnotic against some dizzyingly plush production, but a modern spin on 80s pastiche sometimes veers too close to tribute Swedish-Iranian singer Snoh Aalegra has previously described her music – a lush, pastiche-y mix of R&B, hip-hop, soul and pop – as “cinematic soul”. But although she’s a dab hand at graceful, timeless presentation (and has a truly remarkable voice) Aalegra’s music has often struggled to match up to its aesthetic, hampered by her love of the greats and a penchant for broadly generic lyrics. Her most recent album, 2021’s Temporary Highs in the Violet Skies , made some headway toward carving out a more distinctive sound, thanks to sparky and inventive production from Tyler, the Creator, No ID, P2J and the Neptunes, but still didn’t quite feel like the right fit. Aalegra’s fourth album is her most successful front-to-back statement yet, even if she can’t shake off the talent-show-ish reverence for her idols. Sparse and warm

item.title: The beautiful game: revived art prize gives football its creative due once more | Emma John
item.description: Football and the art world have long remained distant but the breadth of entries for this year’s award reveals a healthy revival It may be the Beautiful Game, but in its early decades football was a rare subject for artists. The Italian Futurist Umberto Boccioni whirled an athlete’s body into a vortex of movement in his 1913 painting Dynamism of a Soccer Player . You can see one of the earliest fine art depictions of a match – a smoggy, factory-adjactent scene called Any Wintry Afternoon in England – at the Manchester Art Gallery. If 1930s abstraction is more your thing, you can enjoy decoding the geometric shapes in Kazimir Malevich’s Painterly Realism of a Football Player – Color Masses in the 4th Dimension. I’m guessing the small green pea shape is a ball. These, in any case, were exceptions. In 1953 the Football Assocition launched an art prize, backed by the newly formed Arts Council: the winning works included Going To The Match by LS Lowry, with its crowds flocking to Bolton Wan

item.description: The US reporter wrongly imprisoned for espionage writes compellingly about his ordeal Evan Gershkovich is the Wall Street Journal reporter who, in the early phase of Putin’s war in Ukraine, was snatched up by the Russian authorities on bogus espionage charges and spent a year and a half in Russian jails (first Lefortovo and then Yekaterinburg) before being released in a prisoner exchange in 2024. The opening section of his book about the experience is gripping and rather moving. He recounts his arrest in a sting operation, after meeting a contact who promised to supply him with information about Russia’s military-industrial preparations. Born to Russian Jewish immigrant parents in the US, Gershkovich grew up in suburban New Jersey on a diet of Soviet cartoons and “Krylov’s fables rather than Aesop’s”; he was betwixt and between. item.title: Jess Cartner-Morley on fashion: this season’s big idea? Wear a skirt. It’s that simple
item.description: All you need to look on-trend this autumn is a skirt, but instead of going shopping, check what you already have in your wardrobe I go to a lot of fashion shows, and sometimes they are gorgeous and sometimes they are ugly. Sometimes they are electrifying and sometimes they are deathly dull. Sometimes they are completely baffling. My absolute favourite kind of show is the one that makes me want to run home and change my outfit. A show that makes me think: there it is! That’s exactly what I want to wear. When the look speaks to me, as if it had been on the tip of my tongue. God, I love that. Which is what happened at Prada this season . The idea was: skirts. That’s it, that’s the whole idea. The show was 63 different skirts – some with a sweater, some with a bra top, some with a jacket, but the point was the skirts. item.title: Energy drinks linked to 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest
item.description: A new study found that energy drinks and stimulant supplements were linked to disproportionately frequent reports of serious heart problems, including 11 times more reports of cardiac arrest and 4.5 times more reports of heart attacks. Young adults accounted for nearly half of the cardiovascular reports involving these products, raising concerns about their potential risks despite the study being unable to prove causation.

item.title: Obesity linked to up to 27% lower risk of death in dementia
item.description: A surprising study of more than 4,500 older adults found that people who were overweight or obese when diagnosed with dementia had a 16% to 27% lower risk of death than those at a normal weight. Researchers suspect that extra energy and muscle reserves may help patients survive the disease's toll on the body, although the reason for the survival advantage remains unclear.

item.title: The mystery of how hair knows where to grow may finally be solved
item.description: Scientists have discovered that the intricate patterns of hair follicles on mammals may arise from a remarkably simple process involving cells following chemical signals. The findings challenge a long-standing theory and reveal how nature can create complex biological patterns without a detailed blueprint.

item.title: Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis
item.description: One in five people have experienced this frightening state – and the Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal has dedicated his career to studying it. Could it be a portal to a deeper understanding of the mind? The Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal is considering the unfathomable depths of the human brain. “It can contemplate itself, and vast galaxies, spirits, souls, poetry, Einstein. Yet you hold it in your hand and it seems so trivial.” Jalal’s passion – the subject that drove him to become a scientist – is sleep paralysis, a brain glitch that can fill its host with terror so palpable that it can cause lasting trauma. “What you get very close to in sleep paralysis,” he says, “is that subjective world of the mind. It’s very hard to put into words.” He should know – he’s spent 271 pages trying to do so. His new book, The Phantom Mind, argues that by exploring the borderlands of sleep, where sleep paralysis occurs, we can delve deeper into how all aspects of our minds work. He may wear a

item.title: Proposed approach for diagnosing obesity outperforms old method
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03425-0 A framework for diagnosing obesity that was proposed in 2025 incorporates waist circumference and related measures and distinguishes clinical from preclinical obesity on the basis of obesity-induced organ dysfunction. In an international multi-cohort study of 844,108 adults, this framework outperformed conventional body-mass-index-based criteria in diagnosing obesity and stratifying mortality risk.

item.title: Personal incentives for public officials drove a drop in China’s fertility
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03274-x Once the promotion prospects of bureaucrats became tied to birth targets, the country’s one-child policy became more effective. Can the state now reverse this effect?

item.title: Can green technologies deliver energy security in an unstable world?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03409-0 As global energy markets grapple with a period of sustained political volatility, researchers are digging deep for solutions.

item.title: Human replisomes direct a dedicated leading-strand primase for fork restart
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11204-0 Structural and biochemical studies show that the CMG helicase directly recruits PRIMPOL for leading-strand repriming, enabling replication fork restart and limiting post-replicative DNA gaps.

item.title: Bureaucratic incentives shaped effectiveness of the one-child policy in China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11232-w Stronger bureaucratic incentives under China’s one vote veto policy intensified enforcement of the one-child policy, accounting for nearly half of China’s fertility decline during the 1990s.

item.title: Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11237-5 A large-scale data analysis assesses the Lancet Commission’s proposed diagnostic framework for obesity, finding that this framework, in which BMI is combined with other criteria, such as waist circumference and organ function, is more useful than classifications based on BMI alone.

item.title: UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11256-2 TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact and suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication; a therapeutic strategy is found that corrects UNC13A cryptic splicing by using splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides.

item.title: NRF2 is a mechanosensitive checkpoint for NLRP3 inflammasome activation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11324-7 The stiffness of the extracellular matrix is identified as a pivotal factor that influences activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in vitro and in vivo.

item.title: Non-halogen aqueous electrolytes for four-electron iodine conversion
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11282-0 An electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions enables reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes, and is validated in metal–iodine batteries.

item.title: Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11308-7 IL-1β from neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby brown adipocytes in a low-UCP1 state; cold temperature reduces IL-1β via sympathetic nerves, leading to transition to a high-UCP1 state and increased thermogenesis, while higher temperatures have the opposite effect.

item.title: Epigenetic heterogeneity in breast tumours informs diagnosis and prognosis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11230-y Single-cell epigenetic analyses reveal a conserved epigenetic signature across patients that may help identify those at increased risk for disease relapse in breast cancer.

item.title: A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2′,3′-cNMP produced by insect effectors
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11259-z The rice RNA-binding protein NIB1 detects 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide products from insect saliva RNase, forming nuclear condensates that recruit EDS1 to activate defence, revealing a conserved messenger-based immune pathway in plants.

item.title: Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11278-w Flexible tidal turbine blades with passive trailing-edge deformation match the energy yield of active pitch-controlled blades while reducing fatigue-inducing load fluctuations by up to one-third, lowering maintenance complexity.

item.title: Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11280-2 Analysis of a 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, China, reveals a composition suggesting a low-temperature altered basaltic source, that originated from a mantle depleted in the Hadean, was most likely transported to mantle depths through a transient subduction event and partially melted to produce the trondhjemite.

item.title: Human land use drives microplastic abundance in terrestrial wildlife
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11285-x Microplastic burdens in Brazilian tapirs and anteaters rise with human-modified land use and proximity to development, however animals in remote habitats also carry microplastics, showing that landscape change and individual space use jointly shape wildlife exposure.

item.title: Transient nuclear softening for zygotic gene activation in mice
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11240-w A distinct physical nuclear state acquired by embryos at the beginning of life supports the initiation of the zygotic transcription program.

item.title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11264-2 Experiments in mouse models show that immunoglobulin A in the gut lumen has a role in regulating the turnover of colon epithelial cells and reduces the susceptibility of mice to colorectal cancer.

item.title: Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11269-x The somatic evolutionary histories of haematopoietic cells in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia diagnosis show that the clonal dynamics of blood comply with a set of simple evolutionary rules.

item.title: Scale-rich network-based metamaterials
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11191-2 A network-science-based framework that embeds network heterogeneity into mechanical metamaterials is used to produce scale-rich metamaterials that exhibit properties inaccessible to traditional single-scale systems.

item.title: The molecular basis of replication fork restart via repriming by PRIMPOL
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11276-y PRIMPOL is recruited to stalled forks through an interaction with the replicative helicase CDC45–MCM2–7–GINS, facilitating primer handover from PRIMPOL to the high-fidelity polymerase ε, minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis.

item.title: Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11262-4 A novel therapeutic modality enforces non-native androgen receptor (AR)–p300/CBP interactions to collapse AR transcriptional programs, producing super-inhibitory, lineage-selective suppression of metastatic prostate cancer and establishing domain-alteration chimeras as a broadly applicable therapeutic strategy leveraging induced proximity.

item.title: Glycosylation and importins liquefy the FG barrier in live nuclear pores
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11258-0 Nuclear pore proteins maintain a fluid, spatially organized barrier through coordinated molecular interactions, explaining how cells achieve selective transport and reconciling competing models of pore structure.

item.title: Severe drought and warming increase the extinction risk of cacti
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11265-1 Severe drought and warming will substantially increase the loss of suitable climatic area for cactus species.

item.title: Low-power 2D CFETs using single-crystal high-κ dielectrics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11272-2 A transferable single-crystal anatase titanium dioxide dielectric enables high-quality interfaces with two-dimensional semiconductors, yielding near-ideal switching, low hysteresis and ultra-low-power complementary transistors and inverters.

item.title: Independent interferometric observable confirms black hole shadow in M87*
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11241-9 An imaging algorithm using closure-invariant formalism and diffusion-based reconstruction applied to supermassive black hole very long baseline radio interferometry datasets enables independent recovery of the ring-like shadow and mass that is free from the usual calibration and imaging assumptions.

item.title: Mitochondrial protein import defects enhance tumour immunogenicity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11249-1 Inhibition of mitochondrial protein import can enhance tumour immunogenicity by promoting mitochondrial DNA release.

item.title: Metasurface waveguides for all-day augmented reality glasses
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11277-x An all-day-wearable augmented reality glasses prototype using a dual-layer metasurface-based waveguide and three matched grating patterns achieves a 30° field of view in an 8 × 8-mm2 two-dimensional eyebox while maintaining high luminance efficiency.

item.title: Astronomers discover hidden alien planet in James Webb images
item.description: A breakthrough in telescope imaging could reveal countless alien worlds that have been hiding in plain sight. Scientists developed a new technique that uses a digital twin of the James Webb Space Telescope to remove the overwhelming glare of stars, making faint exoplanets two to 15 times easier to detect than with conventional methods. The technology has already uncovered a previously hidden planet in existing telescope data and could reveal many more.

item.title: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
item.description: Ever since it crashed on to PC and consoles in the late 90s, GTA has been tearing up the game-making rulebook. We explore how its cultural references, rebel spirit and sprawling sense of freedom make it a definitive work of art In the 00s, when the Grand Theft Auto developer Rockstar Games revealed a new project, video game writers from all over the UK would make the journey to the company’s office in London. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them. After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. This is the context of what we are making, Rockstar was saying, and that is where we belong. Continue reading...

item.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action

The forward is still only 23, yet the days when he was rattling in 12 in a Premier League season for Ipswich have come to seem a very long time ago (and his six games for Manchester City even longer). A season at Chelsea had left him bereft of confidence, an odd mix of diffidence and overaggression, devoid of composure in the box, arms flailing like a broken windmill. But the old gifts have not left him. Both goals on Saturday were the result of great muscular surges and if the first finish seemed essentially about hitting the ball as hard as possible on target, the second was a precise – and still powerful – finish in off the far post. After games such as this it’s possible to imagine him as England’s long-term replacement for Harry Kane. Jonathan Wilson Match report: Nottingham Forest 3

Still, Fifa has already announced that it surpassed its own lofty revenue projections for the 2026 World Cup, bringing in $15bn, significantly more than anticipated. It appears that a third of that total – $5bn – came from ticket sales and hospitality alone, per reporting from the Times . Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the perfect place: back where it all began and where it can all begin again. When Kylian Mbappé scored the first in the clásico on Sunday night, Real Madrid’s manager hardly moved, sitting in the shadow of the bench – but when the striker got the second to win it with time running out, that was different. Mourinho leapt into the light, throwing himself to the grass, the knees of a 63-year-old’s trousers muddy as a schoolboy’s, stuck his tongue out and pumped his fists. He does so love it when a plan comes together. To the right of him, the bench was emptying, subs joining the players in sprinting towards the south-west corner. item.description: Swindon manager has a history of viral outbursts but fans want a united club and manager they can support In Ian Holloway’s often madcap managerial orbit, this was simply the latest in a steady succession of eccentric outbursts. Eyes bulging as he spoke, he boomed the letter “D” and promptly stabbed himself in the chest with an imaginary dagger. Next came the letter “M” alongside a blow from another invisible knife. Finally, a “W” followed by a jab to the heart. “Dead. Man. Walking,” he declared, pausing for effect between words and briefly falling into an Oscar-worthy zombie stupor. “That’s how it feels.” To an offbeat press conference genre containing seagulls following trawlers and self-proclaimed special ones, it was a crazy new entry worthy of its subsequent viral nature. Holloway at his finest. Continue reading...

item.title: Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared
item.description: The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...

item.title: Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row
item.description: The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year. Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running , but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.
